1.text: Say what a person or thing is with “A is B” (and “is not”).
1. हो connects two things: A = B
It links a noun to another noun. Nepali does not make the same plain-versus-polite distinction in this word as Japanese does, but its form changes with the subject.
3. Affirmative and negative: the negative is होइन
- **Raise your voice at the end to ask a question**: यो सुन्तला **हो?** (Is this an orange?)
- You can answer directly with **हो (yes) / होइन (no)**.
5. जी: a respectful addition to a name
Use it to show respect to the person you are addressing or talking about. It can follow a first name or a family name: **कार्कीजी** (Mr./Ms. Karki).
हो is for **identity or membership: A = B**. For existence, location, and adjective descriptions, use **छ**, introduced next. Keep the pairs together: हो → **होइन**; छ → **छैन**.

2.text: Say that something exists, say where someone or something is, and say what you have.
1. छ expresses existence and location; the negative is छैन
Of the three forms of हुनु introduced here, **छ** expresses “there is / there are.” Its negative is **छैन**.
2. Place words: here, there, and where
These words **already function as adverbs**, so **do not add -मा**.
With a **noun**, however, add the place postposition **-मा (in / at / on)**: टेबल**मा** (on the table), घर**मा** (at home).

rows: There is no book on the table.

2.text: Nepali expresses “have” with **-सँग (with) + छ**, rather than a separate verb meaning “have” in this pattern.

rows: I do not have any money.

2.text: **Choosing between हो and छ is a key step**: identity (“A is B”) = **हो** (negative होइन); existence, location, and state = **छ** (negative छैन).

3.text: Describe a quality or state with an adjective: “Something is …”.
**With an adjective, छ/छैन means “is / is not,” rather than “exists / does not exist”** (the distinction used in CD Express).
Use **हो** from Theme 1 to connect a noun to a noun, and **छ** here to describe something with an adjective. Remember: **हो** = identity; **छ** = existence or state.

4.text: Talk about change and general facts with “becomes” and “generally is.”
1. The third form of हुनु is हुन्छ

Although all three belong to the same verb हुनु, **हो (identity)** and **छ (a current state)** differ from **हुन्छ**, which expresses what **generally happens or becomes true**. It conjugates **like other verbs**; हुन्छ is the third-person singular form.

rows: He became a doctor. (For becoming something by role, use बन्नु.)

4.text: Keep the three uses separate: **हो** = what something is (identity); **छ** = its current existence or state; **हुन्छ** = what generally happens or changes. Use **बन्नु** for becoming something by role.

5.text: Use Nepali postpositions to show how words relate to each other. These work much like Japanese particles; English usually uses prepositions instead.
1. Put a postposition after a noun and write it attached to that word

rows: To; marks a person or object affected
साथी**लाई** (to a friend / a friend as object)

5.text: 2. Possessive forms change with the pronoun

rows: I live at home with a friend.

5.text: **The place adverbs यहाँ/त्यहाँ/कहाँ do not take -मा** (Theme 2). **-ले (ergative)** is needed for past transitive actions (Theme 11). **-लाई** can mark both a recipient (“to someone”) and a person as an object.

6.text: These words form a related group, rather like English “wh-” words. Leave the question word in the position where the answer would go, as in Japanese.
- In a yes/no question **without a question word**, **raise your voice at the end** (यो सुन्तला हो?).
- With a **question word**, you do not need to force a rise at the end. A slight rise can sound gentler.
Unlike English, **do not move the question word to the beginning**. Choose the copula (हो/छ) using Themes 1 and 2.

7.text: Choose the right subject and level of politeness. **The verb form also changes** with your relationship to the person.
2. Three levels of “you,” plus the highest level

rows: Very intimate / to someone lower in status
Small children or very close relationships (**can be rude if used with the wrong person**)
Seniors and people you have just met (**the safest choice when unsure**)
People of much higher status; customer service

7.text: 3. “He,” “she,” and “that person” also change with respect

rows: This person / that person, when pointing; also used for things

7.text: 4. The subject changes the verb ending: all persons, present गर्नु (“do”)

When unsure, use **तपाईं** for “you.” **तँ** is only for very close relationships or someone lower in status and can be rude. For the verb themes that follow, start with **तपाईं (respectful) and म/उ (non-honorific)**, then add **तँ/तिमी** when ready.

8.text: Talk about habits, general facts, and the near future with the present form.
1. Start with the dictionary form and stem
The dictionary form of a verb ends in **-नु** (the dictionary form, or nu-infinitive): गर्नु (do), लेख्नु (write).
Remove **-नु** to find the **stem**: गर् / लेख्.
2. The present covers both habits and the near future

rows: I get up at seven in the morning. (Habit)
I will get up at seven tomorrow. (Future)

8.text: 3. Conjugation across persons: stem + छ-family endings, using गर्नु (“do”)
Note: Verbs with a vowel-final stem, such as पिउनु (drink), use **ँछ**: म **पिउँछु** (piũchu), हामी **पिउँछौं**.
Attach it directly to the dictionary form rather than adding the ordinary stem endings.
5. The versatile verb गर्नु (“do”): noun + गर्नु
Like Japanese “noun + do,” this pattern makes many useful verbs: काम **गर्नु** (work), माया **गर्नु** (love), शुरू **गर्नु** (start).
The present form can mean both “usually do” and “will do soon.” Make the future meaning **clear** by adding a time word such as **भोलि (tomorrow)** (Theme 13).

9.text: Say that you or someone else does not do something.
The affirmative **छ-family** endings change to the **दिन／दैन family** in the negative.
2. The respectful negative is dictionary form + हुन्न
कार्कीजी भात **खानुहुन्न**। (karkījī bhāt khānuhunna = Mr./Ms. Karki does not eat rice.)
To say “do not,” **change the verb itself to its negative form**; do not add a separate word for “not.” The first-person singular uses **-दिनँ**; the third person uses **-दैन**.

10.text: Say that an action is happening right now.
2. It can also describe the near future
म भोलि नेपाल **जाँदैछु**। (ma bholi nepāl jā̃daichu = I am going to Nepal tomorrow.)
3. For “not doing,” this guide uses a perfect negative
This guide treats a negative ongoing situation as no longer in progress and uses the **present perfect negative** (〜पढेको छैन) rather than a progressive negative (Theme 15).
रामले अहिले किताब **पढेको छैन**। (Ram is not reading a book now.)
**पढिरहन्छ** (paḍhirahancha = keeps reading) is a compound verb for continuation, distinct from the progressive (-दैछ).
The progressive uses **-दै + छ** (खाँदैछ). Do **not add -ले** to the doer even in a past progressive; ले belongs to the past completed transitive pattern covered in Theme 11.

11.text: Say what happened in the past. **Here comes -ले, one of the biggest steps in learning Nepali.**
1. Making the past: stem (or alternate past stem) + past endings
2. Essential: add -ले to the doer of a transitive action

For a past action with a verb that **takes an object**, such as eat, read, write, or do, add **-ले** to the subject. Do not add it with intransitive verbs such as sleep, go, or come. Pronouns change form.
3. “Was / were / there was”: थियो, the shared past of ho and छ
The present distinguishes हो from छ, but **both use थियो (thiyo) in the past**.

A common beginner mistake is **forgetting -ले**. For this past transitive pattern, remember “action with an object = subject + -ले.” Some verbs have an alternate past stem (for example, जानु→ग, हुनु→भ/थि).

12.text: Say that an action did not happen.
पैसा **थिएन**। (paisā thiena = There was no money.)
3. Examples: keep -ले in negative sentences too

rows: I did not read a book.

12.text: **Keep -ले on the subject of a transitive verb** in the negative. Do not remove it.

13.text: Say what you will do. **You can use the present form you already know.**
1. Express the future with a present form + a time word
You do not need a separate future conjugation for this pattern. Add a word such as “tomorrow” to the present form from Theme 8.

rows: I will go to school tomorrow.

13.text: 2. For a prediction, add होला at the end
भोलि पानी पर्छ **होला**। (bholi pānī parcha holā = It will probably rain tomorrow.)
The verb form is the same as the present in Theme 8. Put a time expression toward the beginning. For a prediction you are not certain about, add **होला** at the end (Theme 31).

14.text: Describe something you used to do regularly.
1. Pattern: stem + थ्यो-family endings (थ्यो is a contraction of थियो)
This means “used to” or “would regularly.” Attach it to the stem in a similar way to the present endings.
Negative: present third-person negative -दैन + थ्यो → “-दैनथ्यो” (first-person singular: -दिनथें).
2. Examples: no -ले, even with transitive verbs in the habitual past

rows: Ram used to cry a lot when he was little.
Mr./Ms. Dhakal used to visit my home.

14.text: 3. Another pattern: present participle -ने + गर्नु (“do regularly”)
For a past habit, use **-ने गर्थे**.
सिनेमा **हेर्ने गर्थे**। (sinemā herne garthe = I used to watch films.)
Unlike a single past action (Theme 11), **the habitual past describes repeated or regular actions**. Notice that it does not use -ले.

15.text: Say that something is already done, that you have had an experience, or that a result is still true now.
Add **-एको** to the verb stem to make a past participle, then add **छ** to make the present perfect.

rows: I have eaten rice. (I have already eaten.)
I am tired. (I became tired and still am.)
① Completed action with a present effect

15.text: 3. Add -ले to the subject with a transitive verb (the participle pattern also takes ले)
**मैले** सुशी **खाएको छु**। (maile suśī khāeko chu = I have eaten sushi before.)
मैले अझै खाना **खाएको छैन**। (maile ajhai khānā khāeko chaina = I have not eaten yet.)

The progressive (Theme 10) describes an action in progress. This perfect pattern means **it is already done, or its result is true now**. For “have not done yet,” use **-एको छैन**, rather than the simple past negative.

16.text: Say that something had already happened by a particular time in the past.
Simply replace the present-perfect **छ** with past **थियो**.

rows: I had been there / had gone there.
He had already finished reading the book.

16.text: राम त्यस बेला किताब **पढेको थिएन**। (rām tyes belā kitāb paḍheko thiena = Ram had not read the book at that time.)
Keep the time reference clear: **present perfect (-एको छ)** = completed by now; **past perfect (-एको थियो)** = completed by a point in the past.

17.text: Ask someone to do something using an appropriate level of politeness.
2. Add a small word after the command to change its tone

rows: “Go on, try …” (to someone lower in status)

17.text: In conversation, **-नुहोस्** may be shortened to something like **-नुस्**, but **write -नुहोस्**.
When unsure, use **-नुहोस् (तपाईं)**. For “do not,” see Theme 19.

rows: Shall I sit? / May I sit?
Let's not play tennis; let's play football.

18.text: Raise your voice at the end to ask permission: “May I …?” Put **न** before the verb to make it negative (नखेलौं = let's not play).

19.text: Say “You must not …” and “Please do not …”.

rows: ① Polite request to stop / avoid an action
You must not take photographs here.

19.text: In pattern ①, place **न** before the verb (न + हेर्नुहोस् → **न**हेर्नुहोस्).

20.text: Say what you can and cannot do.
**सक्नु** means “can.” The preceding verb takes stem + **न**. The negative shown here is **सक्दिनँ**.

21.text: Say “must / have to” and “may / be allowed to.”
1. Obligation: dictionary form + पर्छ (पर्नु stays in third-person singular)

rows: Had to / did not have to

21.text: Use **-ले** on the subject for a felt personal duty, or **-लाई** for a need imposed by circumstances.

rows: I have to go to the office tomorrow.
I had to get up early.

21.text: 2. Permission: stem + न हुन्छ／मिल्छ／सकिन्छ (“may / be allowed to”)
In this obligation pattern, **पर्नु takes पर्छ regardless of the subject**. The negative **पर्दैन** means “do not have to,” not “must not.”

22.text: Say what you want to do.

rows: What do you want to do? (Respectful)
I feel like watching a film.

22.text: Pattern ① uses **म**; pattern ② uses **मलाई** (literally “to me”). Pattern ② emphasizes how you feel. Do not confuse it with **मन पर्छ**, “like” (related to the patterns in Theme 2).

23.text: Use adjectives in the right form and position.
1. Position: before the noun, directly before what is being described
ठूलो घर (a big house), पुरानो किताब (an old book).
2. Adjectives ending in -ो change for gender and number
Note: Adjectives with other endings, such as a consonant, do not change; for example, ठिक्क (“just right”).
3. Adjectives can also describe the subject: review of Theme 3
Adjectives in **-ो** take **-ो/-ी/-ा** to match the gender and number of the following noun. Put the adjective before the noun.

24.text: Describe actions with words such as “quickly,” “very,” and “always,” and make exclamations such as “How …!”.
1. Put an adverb before the verb
Examples: ऊ धेरै **छिटो** दौड्छ। (He runs very quickly.) / म **बिस्तारै** हिँड्छु। (I walk slowly.)
**कति** means “how much?” in a question and “how …!” in an exclamation. Punctuation and tone show the difference.

25.text: Say “A is more … than B” and “the most …”.
1. Comparison: B + भन्दा + adjective (“more … than B”)
As a postposition, it is written attached to the preceding word. The order of the compared items can vary.
Note: To compare actions, use dictionary form + भन्दा: बाँच्नु**भन्दा** मर्नु निको (It is better to die than to live).
Do not add comparative or superlative endings like English **-er / -est**. Add “the comparison item + **भन्दा**” or **सबभन्दा**; the adjective does not change to mark degree.

26.text: 2. In a list, use र／अनि only before the final item; use commas elsewhere

rows: yo chiṭo, sasto ani miṭho cha
This is quick, cheap, and delicious.
malāī ciyā ra kaphī man parcha
ū vidyārthī ho tara kām garcha
He is a student, but he works.
I went to bed early because I was tired.

26.text: Repeat **पनि** for “both … and … / … too, and … too.” Put **कोले／भएकोले** at the end of the clause giving the reason.

27.text: Link two actions to show that they happen at the same time or one after the other.

rows: I study while listening to music.
I eat after washing my hands.
I wash my face after getting up.

27.text: **-दै = at the same time** (“while doing”); **-एपछि = in sequence** (“after doing”). The ending changes the relationship between the actions.

rows: I go to the library to study.

28.text: Use **नको लागि** with a verb and **को लागि** with a noun. Put the purpose before the main action.

29.text: Describe a noun with an action, as in “the person who reads.”
Adding **-ने** to a verb stem makes a present participle. Put it before the noun to mean “the person / thing that does …”.
पैसा **पाउने बित्तिकै** हरि पोखरा गयो। (paisā pāune bittikai hari pokharā gayo = As soon as Hari got the money, he went to Pokhara.)
The action describing the noun comes **before the noun**, as in Japanese. This is the reverse of an English “noun + who / that …” relative clause.

30.text: 1. Pattern: condition + भने, then the result
Put **भने** (“if”) after the condition. You can add **यदि (“if”) at the beginning, but it is optional**.

rows: If Ram comes, Shyam will go.
If Ram is coming, Shyam will go.
If it is cheap, I will buy it.

30.text: **Keep भने**; यदि is optional. The condition can use a past form (आयो भने) or a present form (आउँछ भने).

31.text: Say “probably” and “I think,” with different degrees of certainty.
1. “It seems / I think”: sentence + जस्तो लाग्छ
भोलि पानी पर्छ **जस्तो लाग्छ**। (bholi pānī parcha jasto lāgcha = I think it will rain tomorrow.)
भोलि पानी पर्छ **होला**। (bholi pānī parcha holā = It will probably rain tomorrow.)
Note: **सायद (“perhaps / probably”)** goes at the beginning and is often used with होला.
3. “Must have / must be”: past participle + हुनु पर्छ

rows: Shyam must have gone to Europe.
Ram must have a lot of money.

31.text: भोलि पानी **पर्न सक्छ**। (bholi pānī parna sakcha = It might rain tomorrow.)
The certainty scale introduced here is **जस्तो लाग्छ** (impression / opinion) < **होला／न सक्छ** (possibility) < **हुनु पर्छ** (strong inference: “must”).

32.text: Say that something “is done” or “was done.”
यो किताब धेरै मानिस**ले** **पढिन्छ**। (yo kitāb dherai mānisle paḍhincha = This book is read by many people.)
3. An impersonal use: saying a lot was done without naming the doer
आज धेरै **हिंडियो**! (āja dherai hiḍiyo = There was a lot of walking today! / We walked a lot today!) / खूब **खाइयो**! (There was plenty of eating! / We ate a lot!)
“Was done” uses stem + **इयो**. The doer takes **-ले**.

33.text: Say that someone makes or has another person do something.
1. Many verbs form a causative with an ending in -आउनु
2. For a verb without a causative form: stem + न लगाउनु
3. The person made to act takes -लाई; the subject takes -ले

rows: Father made me drive the car.

33.text: In this causative pattern, remember the pair: **the person causing the action = subject + -ले**; **the person made to act = -लाई**.

34.text: In this pattern, there is no separate word corresponding to English “that.” **Put the spoken words first and “said” at the end**.

rows: The teacher said there would be an exam the next day.

34.text: आमाले सधैं भन्ने **गर्नुहुन्थ्यो**। (Mother used to say it all the time.)
You do not need a word corresponding to English “that” in this pattern. **Put the spoken words directly before भन्यो**.

35.text: Look up **every person** using the representative verb **गर्नु (do; stem गर्)**. Other consonant-stem verbs, such as लेख्नु (write) and बोल्नु (speak), follow the same pattern.
0. Person and pronouns: the groups that determine conjugation

rows: Second person, lower status / very intimate

35.text: 2. Past: affirmative and negative; add -ले to the subject because this verb is transitive
3. Present perfect (-एको छ): transitive verbs take +ले; the participle varies as -एको/-एकी/-एका
4. Habitual past (थ्यो): no -ले, even with transitive verbs
This guide uses **the present form (section 1) + a time word**, rather than a dedicated future conjugation: म **भोलि** गर्छु (I will do it tomorrow).
7. Note: some verbs use an alternate stem in the past
गर्नु follows the regular pattern here, but vowel-stem and irregular verbs can change their stem in the past.

Start with **म (-छु), तपाईं (-नुहुन्छ), and उ (-छ)**, then expand to **तँ/तिमी/उनी/हामी/उनीहरू**. Learn affirmative and negative forms in pairs: negatives use the **दिन/दैन family** in the present and the **न family** in the past.

36.text: Check every person for the three “be / exist” patterns: **हो (identity), छ (existence / state), and थियो (past)**.
2. छ: present existence, location, or state
3. थियो: past “was / were / existed,” shared by हो and छ

This is a present form of हुनु and **follows the conjugation pattern of गर्नु in Appendix A**. For general or habitual statements, do not start with म हुन्छु…; focus on third-person **हुन्छ**. The past of “become” is **भयो**.

Distinguish **हो and छ in the present** (negative होइन／छैन), but remember that **both share थियो in the past** (negative थिएन). The respectful forms, **present हुनुहुन्छ and past हुनुहुन्थ्यो**, are shared by हो/छ.
